The Roman Empire, one of the most influential and powerful civilizations in human history, began as a small city-state in central Italy around 753 BC. According to legend, the city of Rome was founded by Romulus and Remus, two brothers who were said to be the sons of the god Mars. The early history of Rome is shrouded in myth, but it is believed that the city was initially ruled by a series of kings, with Romulus being the first. The Roman Kingdom, as it came to be known, was characterized by a system of governance in which the king held absolute power, advised by a council of elders known as the Senate.

As the Roman Kingdom grew and prospered, it began to expand its territories through a series of conquests, incorporating neighboring cities and states into its dominion. The last king of Rome, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, was overthrown in 509 BC, marking the end of the Roman Kingdom and the beginning of the Roman Republic. The Roman Republic was a system of government in which power was held by the people, who elected representatives to make decisions on their behalf. The Republic was characterized by a complex system of governance, with two consuls serving as the head of state, advised by the Senate and the Assemblies, which were made up of representatives elected by the people.

The Roman Republic was marked by a period of significant expansion, as Rome continued to conquer and incorporate new territories into its dominion. The Republic was also marked by a series of conflicts, including the Punic Wars, which were fought against the Phoenician city of Carthage. The Punic Wars, which lasted from 264 to 146 BC, were a series of three conflicts that saw Rome emerge victorious, but at great cost.
